question.text: Scenario: Arun Kumar is analyzing Reliance Industries (RIL) stock using multiple technical indicators. Current observations: (1) RIL CMP: Rs.2,850. (2) 50-day SMA: Rs.2,780 (rising). 200-day SMA: Rs.2,650 (rising). (3) The 50-day SMA crossed above the 200-day SMA one month ago. (4) RSI: 58. (5) Bollinger Bands: Upper band Rs.2,950, Middle band Rs.2,780, Lower band Rs.2,610. Price is between middle and upper band. (6) Strong support at Rs.2,600 (tested 3 times in last 6 months). (7) Resistance at Rs.2,950 (tested twice). (8) Volume has been above average on recent up-days. (9) MACD is above the signal line and above the zero baseline. Question 4 of 5: With the stock between the middle and upper Bollinger Band, the interpretation is:

answer.text: The stock has positive momentum — trading in the upper half of the normal range suggests bullish bias
The stock is about to crash
Bollinger Bands are not applicable to individual stocks

explanation.text: The Logic: Bollinger Bands plot a middle line (a moving average, here Rs. 2,780) with an upper and lower band placed a fixed number of standard deviations above and below. When price trades in the upper half of the envelope — between the middle band and the upper band — it is generally read as evidence of positive momentum and a bullish bias, because closes are persistently above the moving average. The upper band itself signals potential short-term overextension; the lower band signals potential support or oversold conditions. The Trap: "Extremely oversold" is the opposite reading — oversold tags are associated with price near or below the lower band. "About to crash" is not the standard inference from trading in the upper half of the bands. Bollinger Bands are widely applied to individual liquid stocks, so calling them inapplicable is incorrect. Note: The specific interpretation that price between the middle and upper band signals positive momentum/bullish bias is not stated on the cited NISM Series XV Research Analyst pages checked (pp.312-326; p.313 references Bollinger Bands only as one tool for support and resistance identification). The interpretation above reflects general industry technical-analysis usage rather than the cited workbook chapter.
